newsitem.title: USA: Clinton whips Dole, Republicans hang on to Congress.
newsitem.headline: Clinton whips Dole, Republicans hang on to Congress.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, dismissed as irrelevant two years ago, basked in the glory of a sweeping re-election victory on Wednesday but faced strong opposition as Republicans held on to Congress.

"No words can convey the gratitude I feel tonight for the honour that has been given to me," Clinton told happy throngs in Little Rock, Ark., after winning most of the country's most populous states on Tuesday and piling up 379 Electoral College votes to 159 for Republican Bob Dole. The winner needed 270.

But partisan battles between the White House and Capitol Hill, including fighting over alleged Clinton administration ethical abuses, were guaranteed after an election that was if anything a victory for the status quo.

Republicans easily held on to the Senate and clung to control of the 435-seat House of Representatives. Speaker Newt Gingrich early on Wednesday predicted a Republican loss of five to 10 seats. The Democrats needed 19 to seize control.

Clinton's re-election represented a remarkable comeback two years after he was pronounced politically irrelevant when voters, in what was seen as a mid-term referendum on his presidency, ousted his Democrats from control of Congress.

After suffering the ignominy of having won with only 43 percent of the vote in 1992, Clinton was particularly gratified at receiving about 50 percent of the vote this time, apparently avoiding becoming the first two-time plurality president since Woodrow Wilson early this century.
With 81 percent of election precincts reporting, Clinton had 50 percent of the vote to 42 percent for Dole and eight percent for Perot.

Television networks said the election -- which many Americans rated as boring -- attracted less than 50 percent of eligible voters, a record low turnout. The previous lowest turnout in a presidential election was 50.1 percent in 1988.
Computerized voter tallies by the networks projected Clinton the winner in 31 of the 50 U.S. states plus the District of Columbia, to 19 states for Dole.
Dole, 73, the former Senate majority leader from Kansas whose campaign had difficulties from the beginning, conceded defeat with aplomb.

"It hurts to lose an election, but stay involved and keep fighting the good fight," Dole told cheering supporters at a hotel in Washington. Echoing a statement he made throughout his campaign, he added, "I'm still the most optimistic man in America."
Nonetheless, he was misty-eyed at the loss. "I was just thinking in the elevator on my way downstairs, tomorrow will be the first time in my life I don't have anything to do," he said.

Clinton, flanked by wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea, 16, and Vice President Al Gore and Tipper Gore, celebrated his election victory in a speech in Little Rock at the Old State House -- a large white Greek Revival structure where he first announced his run for the presidency in 1992.
In a long victory statement that sounded at times like an inaugural address, Clinton appealed for an end to partisanship.

"It is time to put country ahead of party ... They (the voters) are sending us a message -- work together, meet our challenges, put aside the politics of division and build America's community together," he said.

Winning Congress for a second consecutive term for the first time in 68 years, Republicans will keep control of the congressional committees investigating a wide range of alleged Clinton administration wrongdoing.

They made clear they would pursue a wide range of inquiries into the president's political, business and personal affairs. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said voters were sending a Republican Congress back to keep Clinton under political lock and key.
These include the complex Whitewater affair, the mishandling of the FBI files of some prominent Republicans and revelations on campaign fundraising from foreign interests.

Oklahoma Republican Sen. Don Nickles said Republican control of Congress was "good news for cleaning up government when we find that people are making mistakes in the White House. We're going to start watching them a little bit closer now."

The Republicans kept the Senate by winning open seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and Clinton's home state of Arkansas. They expanded their majority in the 100-seat chamber by at least one seat to 54-45 with one race in Oregon still undecided.
Among those winning was South Carolina's living legend, 93-year-old Strom Thurmond, who easily won an unprecedented eighth term by whipping a Democratic challenger 50 years his junior.
The key to Clinton's victory seemed clearly to be that voters rated personal security and national prosperity far above the character issues and tax-cut promises Dole pushed.

ABC News reported 58 percent of those leaving the polls rated the economy in good shape. That compared with only 19 percent four years ago, when Clinton ousted Republican George Bush by hammering at discontent with a weak economy.
